scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Mak Sa'moa, which translates to 'Samoan dance' in Rotuman, originated from Samoan movement styles introduced by early ancestors such as Raho, whom Rotumans venerate as the founder of their islands.

Although long performed as a customary Rotuman dance, islanders only realized its explicit Samoan origin following interaction with London Missionary Society and Methodist Church missionaries in the modern era.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Mak Sa'moa is commonly performed during the av' mane'a season as part of the Rotuman fara festivities.
It serves as a valued social expression, particularly among older generations who cherish its links to ancestral history and measured musical pace.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed informally with interactions between male and female partners.

The core movement mechanics rely on hand movements exchanged between man and woman, accompanied by footwork where dancers shuffle and twist their feet inward and outward, recalling the movement patterns of the Siva Samoa.
The overall execution follows a deliberate, generally slower pace.
Watch for Foot shuffling and twisting.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Raho, the legendary founder of Rotuma, is cited in oral tradition as one of the early Samoan ancestors from whom the dance form was derived.
Mak Sa'moa derives from early Samoan dance traditions, specifically carrying movement patterns shared with the Samoan Siva Samoa, adapted into Rotuman informal social dance.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Mak Sa'moa is parent of Siva Samoa: Mak Sa'moa derives its footwork and hand movement patterns from early Samoan ancestral dance forms like Siva Samoa.
Mak Sa'moa is sibling of Mak Rarotoga: Another borrowed dance form on Rotuma, contrasted with Mak Sa'moa due to its faster Tahitian/Rarotongan style tunes.
